name: main
prose: Entry point of sdiff. Precondition: argv is the command line. It sets exit_failure = EXIT_TROUBLE (2), initialises locale, text domain and c_stack_action(cleanup), reads the EDITOR environment variable into editor_program, and makes the first diff argument DEFAULT_DIFF_PROGRAM. Options are parsed with getopt_long and mostly forwarded to the diff child by diffarg (-a, -b, -B, -d, -E, -H, -i, -I pattern, -l, -t, -w -> -W, -W -> -w, --strip-trailing-cr, --tabsize); -o records the output file, -s sets suppress_common_lines, --diff-program replaces argument 0; -v prints version information and --help prints usage, each followed by check_stdout() (which fails fatally on a write error or on fclose failure) and returns EXIT_SUCCESS; an unknown option calls try_help (which terminates with status EXIT_TROUBLE). If the number of operands is not exactly two, try_help prints a diagnostic and terminates with EXIT_TROUBLE. Without -o it appends --suppress-common-lines (if requested), -y, -- and the two file names and calls execvp on the diff program; if execvp returns, perror_fatal ends the process (exiterr, status 2). With -o: both operands being directories is fatal; it expands the names, opens the left and right files and the output with ck_fopen (fatal on failure), starts diff --sdiff-merge-assist as a child connected by a pipe (or popen when fork/vfork is unavailable; pipe, fork, fdopen and popen failures are fatal), runs interact() on the three streams, closes left, right and out, waits for the child (waitpid retried on EINTR, other errors fatal; pclose in the popen build), removes the temporary file tmpname if any, and then: if interact() returned false it calls exiterr(), which exits with EXIT_TROUBLE; otherwise check_child_status requires a normal exit status of at most EXIT_FAILURE (anything else is reported and ends with exiterr), and the process exits with the child's exit status via exit(WEXITSTATUS(wstatus)). The trailing 'return EXIT_SUCCESS' is not reached.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: the interact_ok == false path exits through exiterr() with status 2 instead of the child's status (sdiff.c:739-740). Slice cut the head only; function name matches.

name: print_sdiff_hunk
prose: Slice cut the head: this is the tail of print_sdiff_hunk(hunk) (side.c:235); there is no function called print_1sdiff_hunk. Precondition: hunk is a change-script node chain and the global line buffers, next0/next1, outfile and the sdiff options are set. It calls analyze_hunk to get the changes kind and the line ranges first0..last0 and first1..last1; if the kind is 0 (UNCHANGED) it returns without printing. Otherwise it first calls print_sdiff_common_lines(first0, first1), which prints the common lines before the hunk (unless suppress_common_lines) and advances next0 and next1; with sdiff_merge_assist it prints a 'c<len0>,<len1>' line; for a CHANGED hunk it prints paired lines with '|' while both ranges have lines, then continues with the remaining kind (OLD or NEW) and sets next0 and next1 to the lines consumed so far; for lines only in the second file it prints them with '>' and sets next1 past them; for lines only in the first file it prints them with '<' and sets next0 past them. It returns nothing.
note: Dropped earlier only because the packet name did not match a function; the slice is the end of print_sdiff_hunk.

name: Info_Out
prose: Interprets a terminfo-style output string (the non-termcap branch of new_curse.c) and writes the result to stdout. Precondition: string is NULL or a NUL-terminated capability string; p_list is NULL or has at least place readable ints; place is at most 9 (p[] has 10 entries). If string is NULL it returns at once without touching p[], Otemp or stdout. Otherwise it clears p[0..9], and, only if p_list is not NULL, fills p[1], p[2], ... from p_list in reverse order (p[1] = p_list[place-1], p[2] = p_list[place-2], and so on, consuming place entries). It then sets the global Otemp to string and walks it: literal characters are written with putchar; '%' sequences are handed to Operation() (printing %d-style numbers, arithmetic and comparison operators on a stack, %c, %i, %p<n>, %P<v>, %g<v>, %'c', %{n} and %%); the conditional forms %? ... %t ... %e ... %; are evaluated by the code in Info_Out itself, skipping the branch that is not selected; '$<n>' computes a padding count from n milliseconds (using chars_per_millisecond) and writes that many copies of the pad character from String_table[pc__] (or 0 when there is none). At the end it calls fflush(stdout). The globals p[], variable[], Otemp, chars and the file-scope stacks are modified. For a well-formed string Otemp ends pointing at the terminating NUL; for malformed strings (an unterminated '$<', '%{' or %' sequence or an unterminated conditional) the scanning loops can read past the end of the string, and the stacks (128 entries) are not bounds-checked.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: p[] is filled from p_list only when p_list is not NULL (new_curse.c:1936-1941); the old prose also had the fill order reversed. Prose qualified for malformed strings.

name: Get_key
prose: Decodes a terminal key sequence that started with first_char (ESC or Ctrl-_), called from wgetch. Precondition: KEY_TOS is NULL or a valid KEY_STACK list of entries with NUL-terminated element->string, Max_Key_len <= 127 (the local buffer string[128]), and standard input is readable through wgetch(stdscr). It puts first_char in string[0], sets Time_Out = FALSE and Noblock = TRUE; in builds without BSD_SELECT it installs Clear as the SIGALRM handler (the old handler is not restored) and starts a one-second alarm. It then reads characters with wgetch(stdscr) (which can itself call Get_key again for another ESC) while fewer than Max_Key_len characters are collected, Time_Out is not set and no match was found; each character other than -1 is appended and the whole accumulated string is compared with every KEY_STACK entry's string with strcmp, taking the first match; the string consisting of first_char alone is never compared, so an entry equal to first_char alone is never returned. After the loop (no BSD_SELECT) it calls alarm(0) if no time-out occurred; in non-SYS5 builds it calls ioctl(0, TIOCSETP, &Terminal) on every return; in SYS5 builds the corresponding ioctl is commented out and the local Gterminal changes are never applied. It sets Noblock = FALSE. If a match was found it returns that entry's element->value; otherwise it pushes back with ungetch, from the last read back to index 1, every collected character except those equal to -1 or 255, and returns first_char.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: no comparison is made before at least one more character has been read (new_curse.c:2386-2399), so a one-character entry equal to first_char cannot match; the old prose did not say so. Old round-2 claim about SYS5 termio changes was already handled (Gterminal is a local that is never applied).

name: Delete_line
prose: Slice cut the head: the function is Delete_line(row, end_row, window) (new_curse.c:3033). Precondition: window is a valid WINDOW and the doubly linked screen-line list starting at curscr->first_line is long enough that the unchecked walks (window->SR links from the head, then row more links) never reach a NULL next_screen. Behaviour: it finds the line at index SR + row (setting the global top_of_win to the window's first line on the way; if row + SR == 0 it first sets curscr->first_line to the next line), unlinks it from the list, clears it with clear_line(tmp1, 0, window->Num_cols), sets its number to -1, and re-inserts it before the line reached by walking up to SR links from curscr->first_line (stopping early at the last line) and then up to end_row further links (again stopping early at the last line), changing only the prev_screen/next_screen fields of the line and its new neighbours (no nodes are allocated or freed). It then positions the terminal at (SR + row, 0) and calls String_Out with the dl__ string; afterwards, if the cs__ string is NULL and end_row < window->Num_lines, it positions at (SR + end_row, 0) and calls String_Out with al__, else if cs__ is non-NULL and dl__ is NULL it positions at (SR + end_row, 0) and outputs a newline. Return value: the line that followed the deleted line before re-insertion (NULL if the deleted line was the last node), except that if row == window->Num_lines - 1 the re-inserted cleared line itself is returned; when row + SR == 0 it also sets curscr->first_line and the global top_of_win to the returned pointer.
note: Dropped earlier for name reasons. Old prose errors: top_of_win is a global, not a local; 'always returns a struct _line pointer' contradicted its own NULL return.

name: HASH_JEN_MIX
prose: Function-like macro HASH_JEN_MIX(a,b,c) (not a C function): it expands to do { ... } while (0) and applies Bob Jenkins' nine-step mixing sequence in place, each step of the form x -= y; x -= z; x ^= (z >> n) or (y << n) with the shift amounts 13, 8, 13, 12, 16, 5, 3, 10, 15 on the three operands. Precondition: a, b and c are distinct modifiable lvalues of an unsigned integer type (HASH_JEN passes unsigned variables and hashv); each is evaluated several times. Postcondition: a, b and c are overwritten with mixed values that depend only on their previous values; with unsigned operands the arithmetic wraps. It returns nothing.
note: Dropped earlier (ensures \true contract). Kept as a fix because the macro performs real computation; it is not a function, so no contract is given.

name: MUR_FMIX
prose: Function-like macro MUR_FMIX(_h) (not a C function): it expands to do { ... } while(0) and applies the MurmurHash3 finalisation mix to _h in place: _h ^= _h >> 16; _h *= 0x85ebca6b; _h ^= _h >> 13; _h *= 0xc2b2ae35l; _h ^= _h >> 16. Precondition: _h is a modifiable lvalue of an unsigned 32-bit type (the shifts assume 32 bits; _h is evaluated several times). Postcondition: _h holds the mixed value, which depends only on its previous value; unsigned multiplication wraps. It returns nothing.
note: Dropped earlier (ensures \true contract). Kept as a fix because the macro performs real computation; it is not a function, so no contract is given.

name: _dwarf_arange_pro_cleanup
prose: Slice cut the head: this is _dwarf_arange_pro_cleanup(dbg) (libdwarf_arange.c:243). Precondition: dbg is non-NULL and dbg->dbg_mode == DW_DLC_WRITE (checked only by assert). If dbg->dbgp_as is NULL it returns without changing anything. Otherwise it removes every Dwarf_Arange from the arange set's as_arlist and frees each one (only the arange structures themselves), frees the arange set head and sets dbg->dbgp_as = NULL. It returns nothing.
note: Dropped earlier because the item was an unnamed fragment; the function exists under the name above.

name: _dwarf_frame_section_init
prose: The packet name _dwarf_frame_section_create does not exist; the array-building code described by the old prose is the end of _dwarf_frame_section_init(dbg, frame_sec, ds, eh_frame, error) (libdwarf_frame.c:440-547), whose tail lies in this slice. Precondition: frame_sec is non-NULL and *frame_sec is NULL (asserted), ds describes a readable section, eh_frame is non-zero for .eh_frame. It callocs a Dwarf_FrameSec (failure sets DW_DLE_MEMORY and returns DW_DLE_MEMORY). It then reads the section entry by entry: a 4-byte length (or 0xffffffff followed by an 8-byte length); a length larger than the remaining data, or a zero length when not .eh_frame, returns DW_DLE_DEBUG_FRAME_LENGTH_BAD (error set); a zero length in .eh_frame ends the loop; each entry is added with _dwarf_frame_add_cie (CIE id 0 in .eh_frame, all ones otherwise) or _dwarf_frame_add_fde, and a non-DW_DLE_NONE result is returned after cleanup. After the loop, if there are CIEs (fs_cielen > 0) it mallocs fs_ciearray and fills it from the CIE list, and likewise fs_fdearray for FDEs; malloc failure returns DW_DLE_MEMORY after cleanup. On success *frame_sec is set to the new section and DW_DLE_NONE is returned; on every failure the section is torn down with _dwarf_frame_section_cleanup (freeing CIEs, FDEs, both arrays and the structure) and *frame_sec is left NULL.
note: Dropped earlier because the name was not in the file. The slice also contains the beginning of _dwarf_frame_run_inst, which is a different function.

name: _dwarf_find_section
prose: Precondition: dbg and name are non-NULL (asserted, so unchecked in NDEBUG builds) and dbg is a valid Dwarf_Debug whose dbg_section array holds dbg_seccnt entries. Postcondition: returns a pointer to the first entry dbg->dbg_section[i], for i from 0 to dbg_seccnt - 1, whose ds_name is non-NULL and strcmp-equal to name, or NULL if there is none; the pointer refers to memory owned by dbg, nothing is allocated or freed and no lock is taken.
note: Reviewer round 15 wrong for this function: _dwarf_find_section (libdwarf_sections.c:209-224) does iterate dbg_section[0..dbg_seccnt-1); the dbgp_seclist STAILQ walk the reviewer saw is the neighbouring function _dwarf_pro_find_section, which is what lies inside the packet slice 252-280. Prose kept.

name: elf_rawdata
prose: Slice cut the head: this is the tail of elf_rawdata(s, ed) (elf_data.c:203), which returns the raw (untranslated) data descriptor of a section. If s is NULL, s->s_elf is NULL or the Elf has no raw file, it sets the ARGUMENT error and returns NULL. With ed == NULL and a non-empty s->s_rawdata list it returns the first descriptor's d_data without allocating; with a non-NULL ed it returns the address of the d_data of the descriptor after ed in the list (taken without a NULL check; because d_data is the first member this is NULL when ed was the last). Otherwise it reads sh_type, sh_offset, sh_size and sh_align from the 32- or 64-bit section header; SHT_NULL sets the SECTION error and returns NULL; for a type other than SHT_NOBITS, if sh_offset exceeds e->e_rawsize or sh_size exceeds the remaining bytes it sets the SECTION error and returns NULL; if _libelf_allocate_data fails it returns NULL (error set by that helper, RESOURCE). Otherwise it fills a new descriptor: d_buf = NULL for SHT_NOBITS or sh_size 0, else e_rawfile + sh_offset; d_off 0, d_align = sh_align, d_size = sh_size, d_type ELF_T_BYTE, d_version = e->e_version, appends it to s->s_rawdata (the section owns it; the caller must not free it) and returns its d_data.
note: Dropped earlier because the packet name _libelf_getrawdata does not exist; the real function is elf_rawdata. The old prose also missed the early returns for ed != NULL and an existing descriptor.

name: elftc_reloc_type_str
prose: Slice is the middle of elftc_reloc_type_str(mach, type) (libelftc/elftc_reloc_type_str.c:35). It switches on the ELF machine (EM_386 and EM_IAMCU, EM_AARCH64, EM_ARM, EM_IA_64, EM_MIPS, EM_PPC, EM_PPC64, EM_RISCV, EM_LOONGARCH, EM_S390, EM_SPARC and EM_SPARCV9, EM_X86_64) and then on the relocation type number, returning a pointer to a string literal such as "R_X86_64_PC32" when both are known. If the machine is not handled, or the type is not listed for that machine, it formats "<unknown: %#x>" for the type into a static 32-byte buffer with snprintf and returns a pointer to that buffer. It never returns NULL; the literals are statically owned, and the buffer is overwritten by the next unknown-type call (so that case is not thread-safe). Callers must not free or modify the result.
note: Old prose said the function returns NULL for an unrecognised machine or type; the code (libelftc/elftc_reloc_type_str.c:955-957) returns the formatted static buffer. Packet name reloc_type_name does not exist.

name: libpe_write_coff_header
prose: Writes the PE COFF header and, when the optional-header size is non-zero, the optional header and data directories, for libpe_write_coff_header(pe, off) (libpe_coff.c:225). Precondition: pe is an initialised PE handle with a writable pe_fd (seekable when pe_cmd == PE_C_RDWR) and off is the file offset of the COFF header. In PE_C_RDWR mode, if neither LIBPE_F_DIRTY_COFF_HEADER nor LIBPE_F_BAD_COFF_HEADER is set it only lseeks past the existing header and skips the write; otherwise it lseeks to off. If pe_ch is NULL it callocs it and picks a default machine from pe_obj; it then sets timestamp if zero, the optional-header size and characteristics by pe_obj (PE_O_PE32, PE_O_PE32P, or optsize 0 for other objects), IMAGE_FILE_LINE_NUMS_STRIPPED, the section count, symbol pointer and count, and IMAGE_FILE_RELOCS_STRIPPED when no .reloc section exists, resets ch_optsize if LIBPE_F_BAD_OPT_HEADER is set, and writes the header with write(). On both paths it advances off past the COFF header, clears LIBPE_F_DIRTY_COFF_HEADER and LIBPE_F_BAD_COFF_HEADER and sets LIBPE_F_DIRTY_SEC_HEADER. If ch_optsize is 0 it returns off at that point. Optional header: in PE_C_RDWR mode with neither LIBPE_F_DIRTY_OPT_HEADER nor LIBPE_F_BAD_OPT_HEADER set it only lseeks forward by ch_optsize and returns off + ch_optsize (flags unchanged); in other modes the flags are not consulted and the optional header is always written. Writing allocates pe_oh (calloc) if NULL, sets the magic, default linker version 2.22, oh_ndatadir = PE_DD_MAX, default alignments and header and image sizes, then writes the fields with WRITE_OPT (a write that would exceed ch_optsize pads the rest and stops; a short write or failed pad fails), may switch pe_obj to PE_O_PE32P when the magic is PE_FORMAT_32P, allocates pe_dd if NULL, fills the base-relocation entry when a .reloc section exists, writes the data directories and pads the rest. At opt_done it advances off by ch_optsize, clears LIBPE_F_DIRTY_OPT_HEADER and LIBPE_F_BAD_OPT_HEADER, sets LIBPE_F_DIRTY_SEC_HEADER and returns off. Failure: it returns -1 with errno EIO (lseek, write or libpe_pad failed) or ENOMEM (calloc failed), leaving already-written bytes and the file position unspecified. pe_ch, pe_oh and pe_dd, once allocated, stay owned by the handle.
note: Reviewer round 15 wrong: the clean-header RDWR path only lseeks (libpe_coff.c:242-253) and jumps to coff_done without writing; the write after lseek happens only for a dirty or bad header or in non-RDWR modes. The old prose was nearly right but implied optional-header flags matter in every mode; I made the RDWR-only condition explicit.

name: libpe_write_msdos_stub
prose: Slice cut the head: this is libpe_write_msdos_stub(pe, off) (libpe_dos.c:208), which writes the MS-DOS header and stub; its second parameter is the file offset off, and strip_rich is a local variable, not a parameter. It returns an off_t offset, or -1 with errno set. In PE_C_RDWR mode: if pe_dh exists and PE_F_STRIP_DOS_STUB is set it sets LIBPE_F_BAD_PE_HEADER and finishes returning the original off; if the DOS header exists and neither dirty, bad nor PE_F_STRIP_RICH_HEADER is set it lseeks forward over the header and stub extension and returns sizeof(PE_DosHdr) + pe_stub_ex (lseek failure: -1, EIO); if the Rich header must be stripped it may read the stub (libpe_read_msdos_stub, result ignored), lseeks to off and marks the header dirty when a Rich header exists (strip_rich); if the header is bad, an application stub of a different size is used, or strip_rich is set, it loads all sections (failure: -1, errno from the callee) and lseeks to off and sets LIBPE_F_BAD_PE_HEADER. Then: with PE_F_STRIP_DOS_STUB it finishes returning off; with an application stub it writes pe_stub_app_sz bytes (short write: -1, EIO) and returns that size; otherwise it callocs and initialises the DOS header if pe_dh is NULL (ENOMEM on failure, marks it dirty), re-initialises it when bad, sets dh_lfanew when stripping the Rich header, writes the header when dirty or bad (short write: -1, EIO) or else lseeks past it (EIO on failure), and then: with strip_rich it lseeks to the start of the Rich header and returns that position; in RDWR mode it lseeks over the existing stub (pe_stub_ex) and returns sizeof(PE_DosHdr) + pe_stub_ex; otherwise it writes the built-in msdos_stub (short write: -1, EIO) and returns sizeof(PE_DosHdr) + sizeof(msdos_stub). Every successful return clears LIBPE_F_DIRTY_DOS_HEADER and LIBPE_F_BAD_DOS_HEADER first; error returns do not. The allocated pe_dh is owned by the handle.
note: Dropped earlier because the packet name libpe_write_dos_header does not exist. The old prose wrongly described strip_rich as a parameter and omitted the early returns of the unchanged-stub and PE_F_STRIP_DOS_STUB cases.

name: dump_dwarf_line
prose: Slice cut the head: this is dump_dwarf_line(re) (readelf.c:4886), the .debug_line dumper. It prints the header 'Dump of debug contents of section .debug_line:' and then returns silently if no section named .debug_line exists, if elf_getdata fails (with a warning only when elf_errno() is non-zero) or if the data size is 0. Then for each compilation unit header returned by dwarf_next_cu_header it searches the siblings for the DW_TAG_compile_unit DIE: if dwarf_tag fails it warns and returns (the DIE found so far is not deallocated), and if no compile-unit DIE is found it warns and returns. If DW_AT_stmt_list is missing it deallocates the DIE and goes on to the next unit; if the unit length does not fit in the section it warns 'invalid .dwarf_line section', deallocates the DIE and goes on. Otherwise it prints the unit header fields (length, version, prologue length, minimum instruction length, is_stmt default, line base and range, opcode base, pointer size), the opcode length table, the directory table, the file name table (entry, dir, time, size, name) and then decodes and prints the line-number program (extended, standard and special opcodes) up to the end of the unit, and deallocates the DIE. The directory and file-name loops scan for NUL terminators without a bound check against the unit end, and the program loop runs while p < pe. After the unit loop it warns if dwarf_next_cu_header returned DW_DLV_ERROR. It returns nothing.
note: Old prose wrongly said an oversized unit length returns early; the code warns, deallocates the DIE and continues with the next unit (readelf.c:4968-4972). Dropped earlier only because the packet name was an unnamed placeholder.

name: addBinding
prose: Precondition: parser, prefix and bindingsPtr are non-NULL, uri is a NUL-terminated string, attId may be NULL and prefix->name may be NULL (default namespace). The caller must remember the old prefix->binding, because success overwrites it (the old value is saved in the new binding's prevPrefixBinding). Checks run in this order and the first failing one returns: (1) uri empty and prefix->name non-NULL: XML_ERROR_UNDECLARING_PREFIX (so this also wins for the prefix "xml"); (2) prefix name "xmlns": XML_ERROR_RESERVED_PREFIX_XMLNS; (3) while scanning uri: len reaching SIZE_MAX returns XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY, and when parser->m_ns is set and uri contains the namespace separator character and that character is not an RFC 3986 URI character it returns XML_ERROR_SYNTAX; (4) if prefix is "xml" and uri is not exactly the XML namespace: XML_ERROR_RESERVED_PREFIX_XML (this also applies when the uri is the xmlns namespace); if prefix is not "xml" and uri is exactly the XML namespace: XML_ERROR_RESERVED_NAMESPACE_URI; (5) prefix not "xml" and uri exactly the xmlns namespace: XML_ERROR_RESERVED_NAMESPACE_URI; (6) a separator is configured and len would overflow: XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY (len is then incremented by 1). It then takes a BINDING from the free list (reallocating its uri buffer with REALLOC when too small; failure or size overflow returns XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY and leaves the binding on the free list) or MALLOCs a new one (failure returns XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY; if the size check after that fails the new BINDING is leaked, and if the uri MALLOC fails the BINDING is freed). On success it copies len characters of uri into b->uri (the last one replaced by the separator when a separator is configured), records prefix, attId and the previous prefix binding, sets prefix->binding to b (or NULL when uri is empty and prefix is the DTD default prefix), pushes b on *bindingsPtr, and, if attId is non-NULL and a startNamespaceDeclHandler is set, calls it with prefix->name and the uri (0 instead of the uri when prefix->binding is NULL), then returns XML_ERROR_NONE.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: the unqualified old claim 'XML_ERROR_RESERVED_PREFIX_XML if prefix is "xml" and uri is not the XML namespace' misses that an empty uri with prefix "xml" returns XML_ERROR_UNDECLARING_PREFIX first (xmlparse.c:4392-4393). The earlier rounds' claims (BINDING leak on overflow check, xmlns namespace with prefix xml) were already reflected.

name: unsignedCharToPrintable
prose: Slice is the middle of unsignedCharToPrintable(c) (xmlparse.c:8777), compiled only when XML_GE == 1. Precondition: none, c is any unsigned char value. Postcondition: returns a pointer to a statically allocated string literal describing the byte: "\\0" for 0, "\\t", "\\n" and "\\r" for 9, 10 and 13, "\\\"" for the double quote and "\\\\" for the backslash, a one-character string for the other printable ASCII bytes (32 to 126), and a hexadecimal escape such as "\\x1", "\\xB" or "\\xFF" (uppercase, no zero padding) for the remaining control characters and for 127 to 255. The switch has a case for each of the 256 values, so the default branch (assert(0); return "dead code") is unreachable. The caller must not free or modify the result; no locks are taken.
note: Dropped earlier because the packet name char_escape_lookup does not exist; the slice is inside unsignedCharToPrintable.

name: condSect0
prose: Static handler condSect0(state, tok, ptr, end, enc) (xmlrole.c:1122; compiled only when XML_DTD is defined) for the token after '<![' in a conditional section. Precondition: state is an initialised PROLOG_STATE; ptr and end are only used for XML_TOK_NAME, where they delimit the token text in encoding enc. Postcondition: XML_TOK_PROLOG_S returns XML_ROLE_NONE and leaves state->handler unchanged; XML_TOK_NAME whose text is the keyword INCLUDE sets state->handler = condSect1 and returns XML_ROLE_NONE, and one whose text is IGNORE sets state->handler = condSect2 and returns XML_ROLE_NONE; every other token, or a name that matches neither keyword, returns common(state, tok). common returns XML_ROLE_INNER_PARAM_ENTITY_REF, without changing the handler, when the state is not the document entity and tok is XML_TOK_PARAM_ENTITY_REF; in every other case it sets state->handler = error and returns XML_ROLE_ERROR.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: common() does not set the handler to error when it returns XML_ROLE_INNER_PARAM_ENTITY_REF (xmlrole.c:1226-1233); the old sentence put both in one clause. The original rejection (PROLOG_S omitted) was already fixed.

name: make_basic_test_case
prose: Slice cut the head: this is make_basic_test_case(s) (basic_tests.c:6602). Precondition: s is a valid check Suite. It creates a TCase named "basic tests" with tcase_create, adds it to s with suite_add_tcase, sets the checked fixture to basic_setup and basic_teardown, and registers the basic test functions on it: 185 direct tcase_add_test calls, 40 through tcase_add_test__ifdef_xml_dtd (registered only when XML_DTD is defined) and 28 through tcase_add_test__if_xml_ge (registered only when XML_GE == 1). It returns nothing; the test case is owned by the suite.
note: Dropped earlier because the packet name make_basic_test_suite does not exist; the registration function is make_basic_test_case. Counts are from the occurrences in basic_tests.c:6602-6876.

name: tmain
prose: tmain (defined as main in xmltchar.h unless wide-character builds) is the xmlwf program entry. Precondition: argv[0..argc-1] are valid strings. Option handling (bundled short options and --): --help and -h call usage(), which exits (status 0); --version and -v print the version and return XMLWF_EXIT_SUCCESS (0) at once; an unknown option or a missing option argument calls usage with XMLWF_EXIT_USAGE_ERROR (4), which exits; an invalid -g, -a or -b value prints a message and calls exit(XMLWF_EXIT_USAGE_ERROR). Other options set processing flags (-r, -s, -n, -p/-x, -w, -m/-c/-t output types, -N, -d outputDir, -e encoding, -k continue on error, -q disable reparse deferral, -a/-b attack-protection limits, -g read size). If no file operands remain it processes standard input (memory mapping disabled). For each input it creates a parser (failure: message and exit(XMLWF_EXIT_INTERNAL_ERROR), 1), applies the amplification and threshold limits (only when XML_GE == 1) and disables reparse deferral if asked (failure exits with status 1), sets handlers, and, for -t clears outputDir, or when an output directory is set builds the output path (an allocation or size-overflow failure exits with status 1) and opens the output file: if fopen fails it sets exitCode = XMLWF_EXIT_OUTPUT_ERROR (3), frees the name and the parser and then either continues with the next file (-k) or stops. It then calls XML_ProcessFile; with an output directory it finishes the meta output, closes the file, removes it if processing failed and frees the name; it frees the parser; if processing failed it sets exitCode = XMLWF_EXIT_NOT_WELLFORMED (2), cleans up the user data and stops unless -k was given. The function returns exitCode, which is 0 only if no file failed; with -k a later file's status overwrites an earlier non-zero exitCode (the last failure wins).
note: Dropped earlier for a mechanical name reason (the definition is spelled tmain). Prose rewritten with the concrete exit paths.

name: get_op
prose: Maps an operator character to a FILE_OP* code. Precondition: c is any char value. Postcondition: returns FILE_OPAND (0) for '&', FILE_OPOR (1) for '|', FILE_OPXOR (2) for '^', FILE_OPADD (3) for '+', FILE_OPMINUS (4) for '-', FILE_OPMULTIPLY (5) for '*', FILE_OPDIVIDE (6) for '/', FILE_OPMODULO (7) for '%', and -1 for every other character. It reads and writes no state.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: the old contract said only result >= 0; the new contract gives the exact code for each character (FILE_OPS is "&|^+-*/%" in file.h:341-349).

name: LOOKS(ascii, t != T)
prose: Generated by the LOOKS(NAME, COND) macro as looks_ascii(buf, nbytes, ubuf, ulen). Precondition: buf points to nbytes readable bytes, ulen is a writable size_t, and ubuf has room for as many file_unichar_t entries as bytes will be accepted (at most nbytes); ubuf is written only for accepted bytes, so it is not touched when nbytes == 0 or the first byte is rejected. Postcondition: *ulen is set to 0 on entry; each byte whose text_chars class is T (the printable ASCII range, BEL, BS, HT, LF, VT, FF, CR, SUB, ESC and NEL 0x85) is stored into ubuf and counted in *ulen; at the first byte of any other class the function returns 0, leaving *ulen equal to the number of bytes copied so far; if every byte is class T (including nbytes == 0) it returns 1 with *ulen == nbytes.
note: Unreviewed earlier; I removed the claim that ubuf is dereferenced unconditionally (the macro writes ubuf only on accepted bytes).

name: LOOKS(latin1, t != T && t != I)
prose: Generated by the LOOKS(NAME, COND) macro as looks_latin1(buf, nbytes, ubuf, ulen). Precondition: buf points to nbytes readable bytes, ulen is a writable size_t, and ubuf has room for as many file_unichar_t entries as bytes will be accepted (at most nbytes); ubuf is written only for accepted bytes. Postcondition: *ulen is set to 0 on entry; each byte whose text_chars class is T or I (class I is the ISO-8859 range 0xA0 to 0xFF) is stored into ubuf and counted; at the first byte of any other class the function returns 0 with *ulen equal to the number of bytes copied so far; if every byte is class T or I (including nbytes == 0) it returns 1 with *ulen == nbytes.
note: Unreviewed earlier; same correction as looks_ascii.

name: LOOKS(extended, t != T && t != I && t != X)
prose: Generated by the LOOKS(NAME, COND) macro as looks_extended(buf, nbytes, ubuf, ulen). Precondition: buf points to nbytes readable bytes, ulen is a writable size_t, and ubuf has room for as many file_unichar_t entries as bytes will be accepted (at most nbytes); ubuf is written only for accepted bytes. Postcondition: *ulen is set to 0 on entry; each byte whose text_chars class is T, I or X (X is 0x80 to 0x9F except NEL 0x85) is stored into ubuf and counted; at the first byte of class F (0x00 to 0x06, 0x0E to 0x19, 0x1C to 0x1F and 0x7F) the function returns 0 with *ulen equal to the number of bytes copied so far; if no byte is of class F (including nbytes == 0) it returns 1 with *ulen == nbytes.
note: Unreviewed earlier; same correction as looks_ascii.

name: file_fsmagic
prose: Slice cut the head: this is file_fsmagic(ms, fn, sb) (fsmagic.c:106), which stats fn into *sb (lstat unless MAGIC_SYMLINK is set, then stat) and reports the file type. Precondition: ms is an initialised magic set, sb is writable. Return values: 0 if fn is NULL; 0 after printing "cannot open `fn' (strerror)" when the stat fails without MAGIC_ERROR (with MAGIC_ERROR it calls file_error and returns -1); -1 whenever file_printf or file_error fails, for an unreadable-link or path-too-long error under MAGIC_ERROR, when the recursive magic_file call for MAGIC_SYMLINK returns NULL, and for an unknown st_mode (file_error "invalid mode"); 1 when the type has been fully reported (directory; character or block device unless MAGIC_DEVICES is set; fifo, door, socket, symbolic link (including broken links through bad_link, which itself returns 1 or -1), a zero-length regular file unless MAGIC_DEVICES is set, and a fifo with MAGIC_DEVICES set reports nothing and still gives 1); and 0 when the file still needs content examination (a non-empty regular file, or a character or block device with MAGIC_DEVICES). When the MAGIC_APPLE or MAGIC_EXTENSION flags are set ('silent') nothing is printed and a result of 1 is turned into 0. With neither MIME nor silent, it prints setuid, setgid and sticky markers separated by commas, then the type text, and a trailing space when ret is 0 and something was printed; in MIME mode it prints inode/... types through handle_mime.
note: Dropped earlier because the packet name fsmagic does not exist; the real name is file_fsmagic. The old prose called sb 'an existing file description' although the function fills it.

name: dophn_exec
prose: Precondition: ms, flags and notecount are valid pointers, fd is an open readable descriptor, and num program headers of size size start at file offset off in a file of size fsize (num may be 0; fsize may be SIZE_UNKNOWN). Postcondition: the function returns -1 only when an elf_printf call fails; every other return is 0: after printing ", no program header" when num is 0, ", corrupted program header size" when size is not the expected program-header size, ", can't read elf program headers at <off>" when reading a header fails (short read), ", can't read section at <offs>" when the pread of a PT_DYNAMIC, PT_INTERP or PT_NOTE body returns -1, immediately when a PT_NOTE header is reached (with sh_num == 0) while MAGIC_MIME is set, and after the loop when MAGIC_MIME is set (no linkage text is printed in either MIME case). Loop behaviour: a PT_NOTE header is skipped when sh_num is non-zero; a header of a type other than PT_DYNAMIC, PT_NOTE or PT_INTERP is skipped when fsize is known and its offset exceeds fsize; for PT_NOTE an alignment with bit 31 set or below 4 prints ", invalid note alignment" and uses 4; PT_DYNAMIC clears the execute bits of ms->mode, sets dynamic and runs dodynamic over its body (updating pie and the need count); PT_INTERP counts a needed interpreter and, unless MAGIC_MIME is set, records the interpreter string or "*empty*"; PT_NOTE passes its body, *flags and *notecount to donote. After the loop (without MAGIC_MIME) it prints ", statically linked", ", dynamically linked" or ", static-pie linked" (dynamic with pie and need == 0), and ", interpreter <path>" if one was recorded. The caller keeps ownership of fd and all pointers.
note: Reviewer round 15 right (narrowly): the skip of headers whose offset exceeds a known fsize applies only to header types other than PT_DYNAMIC/PT_INTERP/PT_NOTE (readelf.c:1782-1788); the old prose stated it for all headers. Earlier-round claims (early 0 returns, PT_NOTE skip via continue) were already reflected.

name: mcopy
prose: Precondition: ms, p and m are valid pointers; s points to at least nbytes readable bytes, except that s may be NULL when indir == 0 and type is FILE_REGEX, and it is not read when type is FILE_OFFSET or offset >= nbytes. Every return statement returns 0. Case indir == 0 and type FILE_DER or FILE_SEARCH: offset is clamped to nbytes if larger; ms->search.s = s + offset, s_len = nbytes - offset, offset = the clamped offset; rm_len is left unchanged; nothing is copied into p. Case indir == 0 and FILE_REGEX: if s is NULL or nbytes < offset it sets search.s = NULL and s_len = 0 (offset and rm_len unchanged); otherwise it sets linecnt = m->str_range and bytecnt = 80 * str_range when REGEX_LINE_COUNT is set in m->str_flags (linecnt 0 and bytecnt = str_range otherwise), replaces bytecnt by nbytes - offset when it is 0 or too large, caps it at ms->regex_max, and sets search.s = s + offset, search.offset = offset and search.rm_len = 0. search.s_len is bytecnt when linecnt is 0 or fewer than linecnt line ends are found; otherwise it is the distance to the position after the last of at most linecnt line ends, where the scan looks for '\n' in the rest of the region first and only if none remains for '\r', treats "\r\n" as one end, and then resumes the search one byte after that position (so the byte right after a line end is skipped by the search; a line end in the last byte leaves the position at that byte). Case indir == 0 and FILE_BESTRING16 or FILE_LESTRING16: if offset >= nbytes p is zeroed; otherwise p->s receives a NUL-terminated string of at most sizeof(p->s) - 1 characters taking one byte of each 16-bit unit starting at s + offset (the second byte of each unit for FILE_BESTRING16, the first for FILE_LESTRING16), replacing a NUL byte by a space when the other byte of its unit exists and is non-zero, with NULs written at p->s[sizeof(p->s) - 1] and after the last character. Case type FILE_OFFSET: p is zeroed and p->q = offset. All other cases (indir != 0, or indir == 0 with any other type): the copy size is sizeof(*p), except that for FILE_STRING and FILE_PSTRING with indir == 0 it is m->str_range when 0 < str_range < sizeof(*p); p is zeroed when offset >= nbytes, else min(size, nbytes - offset) bytes are copied from s + offset into p and the rest of p is zero-filled.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: the CR/LF scan skips an extra byte after each line end (softmagic.c:1409-1415: b is advanced past the terminator by the body and again by the loop increment). Also corrected from the old prose: the str_range size limit applies only to FILE_STRING and FILE_PSTRING, not to 'any other type'.

name: file_strncmp
prose: Precondition: s1 points to at least len readable bytes, and to at least len+1 when STRING_COMPACT_WHITESPACE is set (the byte after a consumed whitespace byte is examined); s2 points to at least len readable bytes, or at least maxlen when STRING_COMPACT_WHITESPACE or STRING_COMPACT_OPTIONAL_WHITESPACE is set, plus one more readable byte when STRING_FULL_WORD is set (the byte after the matched run is examined). Postcondition: the result is 0 exactly when len pattern bytes of s1 match s2 under the flag semantics (plain byte comparison when flags is 0, with embedded NULs compared like any other byte; case folding of s2 for STRING_IGNORE_LOWERCASE/STRING_IGNORE_UPPERCASE where the pattern byte is lower or upper case; whitespace compaction for the compaction flags; and, with STRING_FULL_WORD, the further requirement that the byte after the matched run in s2 is NUL or whitespace). Otherwise it returns a non-zero uint64_t: 1 when the s2 window is exhausted before len bytes are consumed (b reaches eb), when STRING_COMPACT_WHITESPACE meets whitespace in s1 but not in s2, or when the STRING_FULL_WORD check fails; else the uint64_t value of the difference of the first mismatching bytes (the s2 byte, case-folded when the folding flag applied, minus the s1 byte), which wraps to a large value when negative. No state is read or written besides the two buffers.
note: Unreviewed in round 15; I rechecked against softmagic.c:2023-2088. Earlier reviewer points (NULs are not skipped; return 1 on compact-whitespace mismatch) are reflected. Prose kept with minor rewording.

name: dtoa
prose: dtoa(d0, mode, ndigits, decpt, sign, rve) converts a double to a decimal digit string (David Gay's algorithm). Precondition: decpt and sign are writable; rve is NULL or writable. d0 may be any double, including zero, infinity and NaN. Behaviour: when MULTIPLE_THREADS is not defined it first frees the string returned by the previous call. It sets *sign to 1 if the sign bit is set (also for zero and NaN) and works on the absolute value. For infinity it returns "Infinity" and for NaN "NaN" with *decpt = 9999; for zero it returns "0" with *decpt = 1; these strings are copied into newly allocated storage (nrv_alloc) and *rve, if non-NULL, points at their end. Otherwise it returns a newly allocated NUL-terminated string of decimal digits with trailing zeros suppressed, sets *decpt to the decimal-point position relative to the first digit (value = 0.digits * 10^decpt), and *rve, if non-NULL, to the terminating NUL. mode selects the digits: 0 the shortest string that reads back to d0 (round-nearest), 1 the same with Steele-White stopping, 2 max(1, ndigits) significant digits, 3 ndigits digits after the decimal point (ndigits may be negative; a result with no digits is the empty string with *decpt = -ndigits, and a value that rounds up to one unit gives "1"), 4 and 5 like 2 and 3 but allowed to stop early as in mode 0, 6 to 9 as 2 to 5 without the floating-point fast path; any mode outside 0 to 9 is treated as 0. It first tries floating-point arithmetic when few digits are requested and falls back to multiprecision arithmetic (Bigint) otherwise. The caller owns the returned string and must release it with freedtoa. The code never returns NULL: the Bigint allocator (Balloc) does not check malloc failure.
note: Dropped earlier (name not in slice). Old prose said d must be finite and that allocation failure returns NULL or exits; the code handles infinity and NaN explicitly and never checks for allocation failure (misc.c Balloc). I read the control flow and the documented mode semantics of this function, but did not re-derive the multiprecision digit generation (lines 520-735) line by line.

name: gdtoa
prose: The packet name dtoa is wrong; this is gdtoa(fpi, be, bits, kindp, mode, ndigits, decpt, rve), the generalised converter that turns a binary number described by fpi (precision fpi->nbits, rounding mode fpi->rounding), the bit array bits and the binary exponent be (value = integer of bits * 2^be) into a decimal digit string. *kindp carries the class and sign on entry (STRTOG_Zero, Normal, Denormal, Infinite, NaN, with STRTOG_Neg) and receives STRTOG_Inexlo or STRTOG_Inexhi at the end. Behaviour: when MULTIPLE_THREADS is not defined it first frees the previous result; it clears the STRTOG_Inexact bits of *kindp. Zero returns "0" with *decpt = 1; Infinite returns "Infinity" and NaN returns "NaN", both with *decpt = -32768; Normal and Denormal produce digits; any other class value returns NULL (the only NULL return) after the Inexact bits were already cleared. For Normal/Denormal it extracts the bits (bitstob), strips trailing zero bits, and a value that turns out to be zero also gives "0". The digit string is newly allocated (rv_alloc), NUL-terminated, with trailing zeros suppressed; *decpt = k + 1 for decimal exponent k; *rve, if non-NULL, points at the terminating NUL; mode semantics are the same as dtoa (0 and 1 shortest, 2 and 3 fixed count, 4 to 9 variants). The rounding direction follows fpi->rounding adjusted for the sign in *kindp; the floating-point fast path is used only for round-to-nearest. On return *kindp |= STRTOG_Inexhi or STRTOG_Inexlo when the digits were rounded up or truncated inexactly. The caller owns the string and frees it with freedtoa. Allocation failure inside Balloc is not checked.
note: Dropped earlier (name not in slice); old prose described a double-based dtoa with mode in {3,5}, which does not match gdtoa. I read the head, the special-class returns, the rounding setup and the tail of this function but did not read the digit-generation middle (lines 345-700) line by line.

name: strtod_l
prose: The slice is a window of strtod_l(s00, se, loc) (strtod.c:85-1076; strtod itself at strtod.c:1078 only calls strtod_l with the default locale), which parses a decimal or hexadecimal floating-point text. Precondition: s00 is a NUL-terminated string; se is NULL or writable; loc is a valid locale (in USE_LOCALE builds the decimal-point string of loc is used). Behaviour: it skips leading white space (tab, newline, vertical tab, form feed, carriage return, space) and an optional sign; a sign followed by the end of the string returns 0 with *se = s00. A "0x"/"0X" prefix is parsed by gethex (unless NO_HEX_FP), a no-number result giving 0 with *se = s00 and no sign. Otherwise it reads decimal digits, an optional decimal point and fraction, and an optional exponent introduced by e or E (if no digit follows the e the exponent is not consumed; an e with no preceding digits gives 0 with *se = s00); with INFNAN_CHECK it also accepts inf, infinity and nan (optionally nan(hex)). The result is computed exactly with floating-point arithmetic when there are at most DBL_DIG digits and the exponent is small, otherwise by scaling and then correcting an approximation with multiprecision (Bigint) comparisons, honouring the rounding mode in builds that define Honor_FLT_ROUNDS. On overflow the result is infinity (or the largest finite value for rounding toward zero in Honor_FLT_ROUNDS builds) and errno = ERANGE (unless NO_ERRNO); when the value underflows to zero errno = ERANGE, and in the Avoid_Underflow path errno = ERANGE is also set when the result is subnormal or zero. The function has a single exit: it stores the end pointer (the first unconsumed character, or s00 if nothing was converted) in *se when se is non-NULL and returns the value negated when a minus sign was read. Bigint allocation failure is not checked.
note: Dropped earlier because the packet name strtod does not match the function containing the slice (strtod_l). I read the parsing head, the fast paths, the scaling and overflow/underflow code and the exit, but did not read the multiprecision correction loop (about lines 580-1040) line by line.

name: strtodg_l
prose: The slice is a window of strtodg_l(s00, se, fpi, exp, bits, loc) (strtodg.c:316-1065), which parses a decimal or hexadecimal number into the binary format described by fpi. Precondition: s00 is a NUL-terminated string; fpi describes the target (nbits, emin, emax, rounding, sudden_underflow); exp and bits are writable with room for (fpi->nbits + 31) / 32 words in bits; se is NULL or writable; loc is a valid locale. Behaviour: parsing is as in strtod_l (white space, sign, "0x" via gethex, digits, fraction, e/E exponent, and with INFNAN_CHECK inf, infinity, nan and nan(hex), the latter through hexnan). It has a single exit that returns irv: the low three bits are one of STRTOG_Zero, STRTOG_Normal, STRTOG_Denormal, STRTOG_Infinite, STRTOG_NaN, STRTOG_NaNbits (a nan(hex) form returns STRTOG_NaNbits itself, not NaN or'ed with it) or STRTOG_NoNumber, optionally or'ed with STRTOG_Neg (set from the parsed sign, cleared for NoNumber), STRTOG_Inexlo or STRTOG_Inexhi, STRTOG_Underflow and STRTOG_Overflow. For no number it returns STRTOG_NoNumber with *se = s00. *se otherwise points at the first unconsumed character. Rounding follows fpi->rounding and the sign. Overflow returns STRTOG_Infinite | Overflow | Inexhi with errno = ERANGE (or the largest finite value as Normal | Inexlo with *exp = emax for rounding modes that do not round away), underflow returns zero with Underflow and Inexlo (sudden underflow, errno = ERANGE) or a denormal with Underflow when inexact (errno = ERANGE). *exp is set for Normal, Denormal and Infinite/NaN (emax + 1) results; the significand is copied into bits only when a multiprecision result exists (so a plain zero parsed from no non-zero digits leaves bits and *exp unwritten). There is no STRTOG_NoMemory return in this source (gdtoa.h defines no such code), and allocation failure inside Balloc is not checked.
note: Reviewer claims: round 1 (omits STRTOG_Denormal) right; round 2 (omits STRTOG_NoMemory) wrong, no such code exists in gdtoa.h:63-80 and the old prose invented it; round 15 right (nan(hex) returns STRTOG_NaNbits alone, hexnan.c:149). I read the parsing head, fast paths, and the overflow/underflow exit in detail but not the whole multiprecision correction (about lines 700-1000).

name: EachMatcherImpl::MatchAndExplain
prose: Precondition: container is a valid Container and listener is a valid MatchResultListener pointer. Postcondition: it calls MatchAndExplainImpl(true, container, listener), which iterates the elements in order, matching each with inner_matcher_ into a private StringMatchResultListener; at the first element that does not match it writes "whose element #<i> doesn't match" (followed by the inner matcher's explanation if non-empty) to *listener and returns false; if every element matches, including the case of an empty container, it writes nothing to the listener and returns true. The writes go through operator<< on the listener, which discards them when the listener is not interested; no IsInterested() check is made here. The container is only read.
note: Reviewer round 15 wrong in its specifics (the code never prints "whose elements all match"), but it is a sign that the old prose was wrong too: the old prose said that an explanation of the matching elements (or of there being none) is appended when everything matches, whereas the all-match path (gmock-matchers.h:2795-2797) writes nothing.

name: MatchMatrix::NextGraph
prose: Precondition: matched_ holds LhsSize() * RhsSize() entries indexed through SpaceIndex(ilhs, irhs). Postcondition: it treats the matrix as a binary counter in row-major order (ilhs outer, irhs inner). It scans entries from the first: each entry that is 1 is set to 0 and the scan continues; at the first entry that is 0 it is set to 1 and the function returns true. If every entry is 1 (or the matrix is empty) it returns false, and in the all-ones case every entry has been set to 0 (the counter wraps to all zeros). It allocates nothing and takes no locks.
